questions.hint: Ask: what do I add to 0 to get 50?

steps.explain: We want a number that, added to 0, makes 50.
Adding 0 changes nothing, so the number must be 50 itself.
Check by subtracting: 50 - 0 = 50.
Why the other answers are wrong: 0 and 5 do not make 50 when added to 0; 100 is too big.

keyPoints.note: Find the missing number: total - the number you have.

questions.stem: Farmer Kim looks after 93 sheep, 75 cows and 57 goats. How many animals does she look after?
questions.hint: Re-order the numbers so two of them make a multiple of 10.

steps.explain: Order does not matter in addition, so choose the order that makes the sum easy: look for two numbers that add to a multiple of 10 (their ones digits add to 10).

questions.stem: How many days are there in September, October and November combined?
questions.hint: Re-order the numbers so two of them make a multiple of 10.

steps.explain: Order does not matter in addition, so choose the order that makes the sum easy: look for two numbers that add to a multiple of 10 (their ones digits add to 10).

steps.explain: Add the first two: 30 + 30 = 60.
Add the next number: 60 + 31 = 91.
Check with the column method in your head (or on paper): the ones, tens and hundreds all add to the same answer.
Why the other answers are wrong: one is 10 too big (a carry was added twice); one is 10 too small (a carry was missed); one is 1 out by a slip in the ones.

keyPoints.note: Combined means add.

meta.note: Uses 30 days in September, 31 in October, 30 in November.

questions.stem: Is your answer to part a more or less than the total number of days in March, April and May? By how much?
questions.hint: Add the days for March, April and May, then compare with 91.

steps.explain: From part a, September + October + November = 30 + 31 + 30 = 91 days.
March, April and May have 31, 30 and 31 days.
Compare the two totals: 91 is less than 92. Find the difference.
So the answer to part a (91) is LESS than the total for March, April and May (92) by 1 day.
Why the other answers are wrong: 'more' reverses the comparison; 'by 2 days' is a slip in the subtraction; 'the same' ignores that 31 + 30 + 31 is not 30 + 31 + 30.

keyPoints.note: Work out both totals, then compare.

Add the tens: 4 + 6 + 1 (carry) = 11 (write 1, carry 1).
Add the hundreds: 3 + 1 (carry) = 4.

questions.stem:
Calculate the sum of the following numbers:
\\(472 + 629 + 254\\)
questions.hint: Line up the digits by place value and add them column by column from right to left.

steps.explain: Add the ones digits: \\(2 + 9 + 4 = 15\\). Write down 5 and carry over 1 to the tens column.
Add the tens digits, including the carryover: \\(7 + 2 + 5 + 1 = 15\\). Write down 5 and carry over 1 to the hundreds column.
Add the hundreds digits, including the carryover: \\(4 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 13\\). Write down 13.
Combine the results to get the total sum.

questions.hint: Line up the place values and add from right to left, carrying over when a column sum exceeds 9.

steps.explain: Add the ones digits: \\(5 + 8 + 4 = 17\\). Write 7 and carry 1 to the tens column.
Add the tens digits and the carryover: \\(4 + 3 + 9 + 1 = 17\\). Write 7 and carry 1 to the hundreds column.
Add the hundreds digits and the carryover: \\(6 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 13\\). Write 13.
State the final sum.

steps.explain: Add the ones digits: \\(4 + 5 + 3 = 12\\). Write 2 and carry 1.
Add the tens digits with carryover: \\(9 + 8 + 7 + 1 = 25\\). Write 5 and carry 2.
Add the hundreds digits with carryover: \\(5 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 17\\). Write 7 and carry 1.
Add the thousands digit with carryover: \\(1 + 1 = 2\\). Write 2.
Give the final accumulated sum.

questions.stem: Andrew helped with the stocktake at the Washer Company. He had to count the number of washers in five different boxes. He counted 1455, 1327, 1604, 1298 and 1576 washers in the five boxes. He then added them together for a grand total of 7030. Was Andrew's addition correct or not? If not, what should it be?
questions.hint: Add the five numbers yourself with the algorithm and compare with 7030.

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

steps.explain: Check with a quick estimate: round each number to its first digit and add. The answer should be close.
Compare with Andrew's total: he wrote 7030 but the correct sum is 7260. They are different, so Andrew's addition was NOT correct (he was 230 short).
Why the other answers are wrong: 'correct' ignores the check; 7030 is Andrew's wrong answer; 7160 and 7360 are slips of 100 in the hundreds column.

keyPoints.note: Do the sum again to check someone's answer.
Line up the place values.

questions.stem: Write the number that is 1805 more than 99.
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (carry when needed).

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

questions.stem:
Find the difference:
\\(73 - 48\\)
questions.hint: Since \\(3\\) is less than \\(8\\) in the ones column, borrow \\(1\\) ten from the tens column.
questions.solution:
Borrow from tens column:
\\(13 - 8 = 5\\) (ones column)
\\(6 - 4 = 2\\) (tens column)

\\(73 - 48 = 25\\).

steps.explain: Regroup the numbers: borrow 1 ten from 7 tens (making it 6 tens) to convert 3 ones into 13 ones.
Subtract the ones column: \\(13 - 8 = 5\\).
Subtract the remaining tens column: \\(6 - 4 = 2\\).
Combine columns to find the final difference.

questions.stem: Write these numbers: 98, 97, 96, 95, 94, 93, 92, 91. Now reverse the digits of each number and subtract the smaller number from the larger number; for example, 98 − 89 = 9. Do this for each number. What are the eight answers?
questions.hint: Subtract for each number: for example 97 reversed is 79, and 97 - 79 = 18.

steps.explain: Reverse the digits of each number and subtract the smaller from the larger:
98 reversed is 89. Larger minus smaller: 98 - 89 = 9.
97 reversed is 79. Larger minus smaller: 97 - 79 = 18.
96 reversed is 69. Larger minus smaller: 96 - 69 = 27.
95 reversed is 59. Larger minus smaller: 95 - 59 = 36.
94 reversed is 49. Larger minus smaller: 94 - 49 = 45.
93 reversed is 39. Larger minus smaller: 93 - 39 = 54.
92 reversed is 29. Larger minus smaller: 92 - 29 = 63.
91 reversed is 19. Larger minus smaller: 91 - 19 = 72.
Write all eight answers in order.
Why the other answers are wrong: a list of all 9s has not carried out each subtraction; a list that ends 9 - 8 - ... counts down by 1; and another reverses the order.

questions.stem: Write these numbers: 98, 97, 96, 95, 94, 93, 92, 91. Reverse the digits of each number and subtract the smaller number from the larger number. What do you notice about all of your answers?
options: They are all the same number, 9.
They are all multiples of 9 (9, 18, 27, ... each 9 more than the one before).
questions.hint: List the answers and look at the gap between them.

steps.explain: From part a the answers are 9, 18, 27, 36, 45, 54, 63, 72.
Look at the gaps between answers: each answer is 9 more than the one before.
So they are the 9 times table: 9 x 1, 9 x 2, 9 x 3, ....
Why the other answers are wrong: the answers are not all 9; 9, 27, 45, 63 are odd but 18, 36, 54, 72 are even; none of them ends in 0.

keyPoints.note: Look for a pattern in the answers.

questions.stem: Try this with other 2-digit numbers (reverse the digits and subtract the smaller from the larger). Do you get the same results? For example 83 and 38.
options: No, and the answers show no pattern.
No, but every answer is still a multiple of 9 (83 − 38 = 45).
questions.hint: Try 83 - 38 and one more example. Is the answer 9 every time? What do the answers have in common?

steps.explain: Try an example: reverse 83 to get 38.
Subtract the smaller number from the larger number.
45 is not 9, so the answers are not always the same. But 45 = 9 x 5, a multiple of 9.
Try another number: 72 reversed is 27 and 72 - 27 = 45. And 61 reversed is 16 and 61 - 16 = 45. All are multiples of 9 because the difference of the digits is multiplied by 9.
Why the other answers are wrong: 'always 9' is only true when the digits differ by 1; 'always 18' only when the digits differ by 2; and the answers do follow a pattern.

keyPoints.note: Compare with the results of part a.

questions.stem: Calculate: $8000 - 2478$
questions.hint: Since $8000$ has consecutive zeros, you must borrow starting all the way from the thousands place ($8$).
questions.solution:
Borrowing steps:
- Borrow from thousands place: $8000$ becomes $7$ thousands, $9$ hundreds, $9$ tens, and $10$ units.
- Subtract: $10-8=2$, $9-7=2$, $9-4=5$, $7-2=5$.

Result: $5\,522$.

questions.stem:
Find the difference:
\\(359 - 64\\)
questions.hint: Subtract the ones column first, then borrow from the hundreds column to subtract the tens column.
questions.solution:
Subtract: 
1. Ones column: \\(9 - 4 = 5\\)
2. Tens column: borrow from hundreds column to get \\(15 - 6 = 9\\)
3. Hundreds column: \\(2 - 0 = 2\\)

\\(359 - 64 = 295\\).

steps.explain: Subtract the ones column: \\(9 - 4 = 5\\).
Regroup the tens: borrow 1 hundred from 3 hundreds (leaving 2) to change 5 tens into 15 tens, then subtract: \\(15 - 6 = 9\\).
Subtract the hundreds column: \\(2 - 0 = 2\\).
Combine column calculations to write the final result.

questions.stem:
Find the difference:
\\(743 - 358\\)
questions.hint: Borrow from the tens column to subtract the ones, and borrow from the hundreds column to subtract the tens.
questions.solution:
Subtract:
1. Ones column: borrow from tens column to make \\(13 - 8 = 5\\)
2. Tens column: borrow from hundreds column to make \\(13 - 5 = 8\\)
3. Hundreds column: \\(6 - 3 = 3\\)

\\(743 - 358 = 385\\).

steps.explain: Regroup the tens and ones: borrow 1 ten from 4 tens (leaving 3) to make 3 ones into 13 ones. Subtract ones: \\(13 - 8 = 5\\).
Regroup the hundreds and tens: borrow 1 hundred from 7 hundreds (leaving 6) to make 3 tens into 13 tens. Subtract tens: \\(13 - 5 = 8\\).
Subtract the remaining hundreds column: \\(6 - 3 = 3\\).
Combine results to get the total difference.

questions.stem: Calculate the difference:\n\\(793 - 147\\)
questions.hint: Subtract column by column. Borrow from the tens column since 7 is greater than 3.
questions.solution:
Perform subtraction:
- Borrow 10 from 9 in the tens column (making 13 in the units column).
- \\(13 - 7 = 6\\).
- Tens column: \\(8 - 4 = 4\\).
- Hundreds column: \\(7 - 1 = 6\\).
- Result: \\(646\\).

steps.explain: Align the digits vertically and borrow 1 ten to make 13 in the units column.
Perform subtraction column-wise.
Combine the column results.

questions.stem: Calculate the difference:\n\\(632 - 248\\)
questions.hint: Borrow from the tens place and then from the hundreds place as needed.
questions.solution:
Subtract with borrowing:
- Units: \\(12 - 8 = 4\\) (borrowed from tens).
- Tens: \\(12 - 4 = 8\\) (borrowed from hundreds).
- Hundreds: \\(5 - 2 = 3\\).
- Result: \\(384\\).

steps.explain: Borrow 1 ten for units column.
Borrow 1 hundred for tens column.
Subtract components of \\(248 = 200 + 40 + 8\\).

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 4 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: The difference means subtract the smaller from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 2: Addition and subtraction

questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

Here: ones: 1 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 4 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 1 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 3 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 2: Addition and subtraction

questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 2 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 1 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

Here: tens: 0 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 1 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 2 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 6 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (16) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 4 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 4 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 4 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 7 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 2 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 1, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Read exactly what the question asks, then choose a method.

Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.

questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 1 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 8 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (18) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 2 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 2 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 2 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 2: Addition and subtraction

questions.stem: The Orange Company took 8435 cases of oranges to the market. It sold 3768 cases of oranges. How many cases were left?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 5 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 4 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: 'How many left' means subtract.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

questions.stem: The Lovely Egg Company normally sells 9750 eggs each week. It has already sold 7995 eggs this week. How many more eggs does it need to sell?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 5 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 7 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Read exactly what the question asks, then choose a method.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 4 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 4 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 6 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (16) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Saving: what is still needed = target - amount saved.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: tens: 4 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 7 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: 'How many left' means subtract.

questions.stem: Adams' Apples has a contract to supply 9250 apples to the market. It has already picked 3878 apples. How many more does it need to pick?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 5 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 2 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Read exactly what the question asks, then choose a method.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: tens: 2 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 1 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 2 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

questions.stem: Calculate the difference:\n\\(91\ 632 - 76\ 218\\)
questions.hint: Align the digits vertically and borrow where the top digit is smaller than the bottom digit.
questions.solution:
Perform subtraction:
- Units: \\(12 - 8 = 4\\) (borrowed 1 ten).
- Tens: \\(2 - 1 = 1\\).
- Hundreds: \\(6 - 2 = 4\\).
- Thousands: \\(11 - 6 = 5\\) (borrowed 1 ten-thousand).
- Ten-thousands: \\(8 - 7 = 1\\).
- Result: \\(15\ 414\\).

steps.explain: Align the digits vertically and perform units column borrowing.
Subtract the lower parts from the borrowed numbers column-wise.
Borrow for thousands column and complete subtraction.

questions.stem: Calculate the difference:\n\\(53\ 462 - 47\ 169\\)
questions.hint: Perform column-by-column subtraction, borrowing from the left as needed.
questions.solution:
Perform subtraction:
- Units: \\(12 - 9 = 3\\) (borrowed from tens).
- Tens: \\(15 - 6 = 9\\) (borrowed from hundreds).
- Hundreds: \\(3 - 1 = 2\\).
- Thousands: \\(13 - 7 = 6\\) (borrowed from ten-thousands).
- Ten-thousands: \\(4 - 4 = 0\\).
- Result: \\(6293\\).

steps.explain: Align the numbers and borrow from the tens and hundreds columns where the top digit is smaller.
Perform subtraction on the lower place values.
Perform subtraction on thousands and ten-thousands places.

questions.stem: Calculate the difference:\n\\(73\ 851 - 68\ 674\\)
questions.hint: Perform subtraction from right to left, borrowing from adjacent left places when needed.
questions.solution:
Perform subtraction:
- Units: \\(11 - 4 = 7\\) (borrowed from tens).
- Tens: \\(14 - 7 = 7\\) (borrowed from hundreds).
- Hundreds: \\(7 - 6 = 1\\).
- Thousands: \\(13 - 8 = 5\\) (borrowed from ten-thousands).
- Ten-thousands: \\(6 - 6 = 0\\).
- Result: \\(5177\\).

steps.explain: Perform units and tens column borrowing adjustments.
Subtract the values in the units, tens, and hundreds columns.
Subtract the values in the thousands and ten-thousands columns.

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

questions.stem: Find the sum of 7, 43 468, 62, 6504 and 793.
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (carry when needed).

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

questions.stem: Find the difference between 70 204 and 31 627.

Here: ones: 4 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 2 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 2, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: The difference means subtract the smaller from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 2 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: tens: 0 is less than 2, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 4 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 3 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 1 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 1 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 2 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 2 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 6 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (16) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

questions.stem: Calculate these subtractions. \(40\,832-26\,338\)
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 2 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 1 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 6 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (16) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 3 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 4 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 5 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 7 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 2 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 4 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 3 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.
Choose a method and check your answer.

keyPoints.note: Work column by column from the right.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 2: Addition and subtraction

questions.stem: Use the algorithms to calculate these money amounts. \(\$8\,000.00-\$3\,365.55\)
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time. Keep the decimal points in a vertical line.

steps.explain: Cents column: there are not enough cents to take 5 away. Trade: take 1 from the thousands of dollars column (the columns in between are 0, so each becomes 9 as the trade passes through) and make 10 more cents. The top digit becomes 10 and the thousands of dollars digit becomes 7. Now 10 - 5 = 5.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 3 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: The difference means subtract the smaller from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 3, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; ten thousands: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 5 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 2 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 3 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; ten thousands: 0 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Subtract: take the smaller number away from the larger.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: hundreds: 3 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; ten thousands: 5 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: The difference means subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.stem: Add ten thousand four hundred and fifty-six to twenty-three thousand and eighty-eight.
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (carry when needed).

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

questions.stem: Tamara's brother has exactly fifty thousand dollars in his bank account. If he buys a new car for $36 895 and pays for it out of his bank account, how much will be left in his account?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: 'How many left' means subtract.

questions.stem: In 1975, George's father paid $28 895 for a flat. In 2000, the flat was valued at $397 000. How much did the flat go up in value during the 25 years?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (trade when needed).

steps.explain: Write the bigger number on top and the number being taken away underneath, with the place values lined up. Work from the RIGHT, one column at a time.

Here: ones: 0 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 0 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 7 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

questions.stem: The Mathsy Theatre has 13 seats in the first row, 15 seats in the second row, 17 seats in the third row, and so on. How many seats are in the theatre if there are 15 rows in all?
questions.hint: Rows go up by 2. The last (15th) row has 13 + 14 × 2 seats. Pair the first and last rows to add quickly.

steps.explain: The rows go up by 2 seats each time: 13, 15, 17, ... Each row has 2 more seats than the one before.

steps.explain: Find the number of seats in the 15th row. There are 14 steps from row 1 to row 15, each adding 2.
Pair the rows from the two ends: the first and last make 13 + 41 = 54, the second and second-last make 15 + 39 = 54, and so on. Every pair makes 54.
There are 15 rows, so 7 pairs and the middle row (27) is left on its own.
Check by adding the rows in order with the addition algorithm.
Why the other answers are wrong: 41 is the number of seats in the LAST row only; 395 and 415 are slips of 10 in the total.

keyPoints.note: Each row has 2 more seats than the one before.
Add the seats in every row.

questions.stem: A spider caught 175 flies in her web in one week. Each day she caught 7 more flies than she did the day before. How many flies did the spider catch on each individual day?
questions.hint: Use the fact that the days go up by 7 each day. The seven days are start, start + 7, start + 14, ... Find the start so the total is 175.

steps.explain: There are 7 days in a week. Each day is 7 more than the day before. Call the first day's catch the 'starting number'.
The extra amounts added to the starting number over the 7 days are 0, 7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42. Add them up.
The total 175 is made of 7 copies of the starting number plus these 147 extra flies.
Take away the extras.
Share 28 equally between 7 days to find the first day.

questions.stem: For which numbers between 1 and 209 do the digits of the number add to 8?
questions.hint: Go through one digit, two digit and three digit numbers in turn. For 3-digit numbers starting with 1, the other two digits add to 7.

steps.explain: One-digit number: only 8 itself has digits that add to 8.
Two-digit numbers: the tens digit and ones digit add to 8: 1+7, 2+6, 3+5, 4+4, 5+3, 6+2, 7+1, 8+0.
Three-digit numbers starting with 1: the other two digits add to 7: 0+7, 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1, 7+0.
Three-digit numbers starting with 2 (up to 209): the other two digits add to 6, but the number must be 209 or less, so the tens digit is 0 and the ones digit is 6.
Put all the numbers in order.
Check one of each kind: 17 gives 1+7=8, 125 gives 1+2+5=8, 206 gives 2+0+6=8.
Why the other answers are wrong: one leaves out 206; one leaves out the 1-digit number 8; one includes 215, which is greater than 209.

keyPoints.text: digits of the number add to 8
keyPoints.note: Add the digits of each number.

questions.stem: Calculate these additions. \(27+14\)
questions.hint: Move some of one number to the other to make a multiple of 10 first.

steps.explain: Make up a ten: 27 needs 3 more to reach 30, a multiple of 10. Take 3 from 14 and add it to 27.

questions.stem: In a magic square, each row, each column and each diagonal should add up to the same total. Work out the numbers missing from each magic square.

questions.hint: Find the magic total first (a complete line, or 3 times the centre). Then find a line with only ONE missing number and subtract the others from the total.

steps.explain: Find the magic total. Every row, column and diagonal adds to the SAME total. Look for a line that is already complete, or use the centre number (the centre is one third of the total).

steps.explain: Find the magic total. Every row, column and diagonal adds to the SAME total. Look for a line that is already complete, or use the centre number (the centre is one third of the total).

questions.stem: What number is 4967 more than 7084?
questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (carry when needed).

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 7 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 3 is less than 6, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: hundreds: 2 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (12) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: 'Less' means subtract.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 2: Addition and subtraction

questions.hint: Line the numbers up by place value and work column by column from the right (carry when needed).

steps.explain: Set the numbers out one under the other, lining up the place values (ones under ones, tens under tens, and so on). Start adding from the RIGHT-hand column.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 7 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 5 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (15) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 1 is less than 10, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Choose a method and check your answer.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 0 is less than 1, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 7 is less than 9, so add 10 to the top (17) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 0 is less than 2, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; thousands: 1 is less than 4, so add 10 to the top (11) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

steps.explain: The 'equal addition' method gives the same answer: when a top digit is too small, add 10 to the top digit and 1 to the bottom digit of the next column. Here: ones: 4 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (14) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; tens: 3 is less than 5, so add 10 to the top (13) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; hundreds: 6 is less than 8, so add 10 to the top (16) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column; ten thousands: 0 is less than 7, so add 10 to the top (10) and 1 to the bottom digit in the next column.
Check by adding: the answer plus the number taken away must give the starting number.
Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.

keyPoints.note: Choose a method and check your answer.

Why the other answers are wrong: one subtracts the smaller digit from the larger in every column (no trading); one is 10 too big; one is 10 too small.
